answer.rationale: The whole case for the mandate-satisfying move rests on memory_c2, which is the single load-bearing and least-checkable claim in the inherited record: it praises the low-cost vendor on unit price, onboarding speed and invoicing accuracy, but says nothing about on-time delivery, defect rates, or whether that experience was at anything like our current committed volume. With the line at 94% and no buffer, a cost-accurate vendor who slips two weeks on a lot is worse than an 18% miss, so I am spending the one verification pull on memory_c2 to see what the original record actually measured and at what volume. memory_c4 (renegotiation recovered margin) is already foreclosed this cycle because the incumbent has refused to reopen price, and memory_c5 (defer) is inapplicable since the contract expires in 14 days and does not auto-renew, so drifting means an uncovered line. memory_c6 (multi-year discount) and memory_c1 (renew for stability) do not reach an 18% cut on their own. That leaves switching primary supply as the only direction that both covers the expiry and meets the mandate, so that is my intended action, but I am scoping it as a small guarded switch: initial volume tranche to the low-cost vendor with the incumbent kept warm as bridge/fallback on short-term terms, explicit delivery-performance gates before any further volume moves, and memory_c3's second-source lesson carried forward as the structure we build toward at next review rather than a single-vendor cutover. If verification shows memory_c2 was a low-volume or short-duration engagement, or that it was scored only on price and invoicing, I will hold the tranche much smaller and treat the cost target as partially met this cycle rather than fully. Residual uncertainty is real and I am not treating the quoted price as a delivered cost.
